title: The Unbreakable Kite
summary: Two friends keep building kites that break during their school's kite-flying day, until they study materials, shape, and wind direction and finally build one that flies.
poll: Trying again after failing is more important than being naturally good at something.

versions.title: The Unbreakable Kite
versions.text:
It was Kite Day at our school. Yousef and Khalid wanted to build a kite and fly it high.

They made their first kite out of paper and thin sticks. Kites can break if the wind is too strong, and that is just what happened. The wind blew hard, and the paper kite tore apart.

They tried again. They made a new kite. It did not break this time, but it spun around and fell down fast. It did not fly well at all.

The two friends did not give up. They asked their teacher, Ms. Reem, for help. She said, "Think about your kite's shape and what it is made of."

Yousef and Khalid looked at their old kites. They saw that thin paper can tear. They saw that thin sticks can snap.

They built a new kite. This time, they used strong plastic and wood sticks. They added a long tail at the bottom.

They turned to face the wind. They let the string out slowly. The kite did not break. It did not spin. It flew high in the sky!

Yousef and Khalid were so happy. They tried many times, and at last, their kite could fly.

They made their first kite out of paper and thin wooden sticks. Kites can break if the wind is too strong. That is just what happened. The wind blew hard. The paper tore. Their kite fell down in pieces.

They tried again with a new shape. But this kite had problems too. It spun around and crashed down fast. It would not fly right.

The two friends did not want to give up. They asked their teacher, Ms. Reem, for help. She told them to think about the kite's shape. She said to think about what it was made from.

Yousef and Khalid looked at their broken kites. They saw that thin paper tears fast. They saw that thin sticks snap in strong wind.

So they built a new kite. This time, they used strong plastic, not paper. They used sturdy wood sticks, not thin ones. They also added a long tail to help it stay steady.

They turned to face the wind. They let the string out slowly. The kite did not break. It did not spin out of control. It flew higher and higher into the sky!

Yousef and Khalid cheered with joy. After trying so many times, their kite could finally fly.

It was Kite Day at our school. The sky was full of colorful kites. Yousef and Khalid decided to build a kite together. They wanted to see how high they could make it fly.

They made their first kite out of paper and thin wooden sticks. Kites can break if the wind is too strong. That is just what happened to theirs. The wind blew hard. The paper tore apart. Their kite crashed to the ground in pieces.

Determined to succeed, they tried again with a different shape. But this kite had its own problems. It spun around in the air and crashed down almost at once. It would not fly properly.

The two friends refused to give up, even after two failed tries. They decided to ask their teacher, Ms. Reem, for advice. She told them to think about the kite's shape. She said to think about the wind and about the materials it is made from.

With this new idea, they built a completely new kite. This time, they used strong plastic instead of paper. They used sturdy wooden dowels instead of flimsy sticks. They also added a long tail to help keep it steady in the air.

They turned to face into the wind, just as Ms. Reem had said. They let the string out slowly and carefully. The kite did not break. It did not spin out of control. It rose steadily and flew higher and higher into the bright sky.

Yousef and Khalid cheered loudly with joy. After trying so many times, their kite could finally fly.

It was Kite Day at our school. The sky above the field was full of colorful kites. Yousef and Khalid decided to build a kite together. They wanted to see how high they could make it fly.

They made their first kite out of paper and thin wooden sticks, shaped like a simple diamond. Kites can break if the wind is too strong for their materials. That is just what happened to theirs. The wind blew hard. The paper tore apart almost at once. Their kite crashed to the ground in pieces.

Determined to succeed, they tried again with a slightly different shape. But this kite made its own problems. It spun around wildly in the air instead of climbing steadily, and it crashed down almost right away. The kite would not fly properly, no matter how carefully they threw it.

The two friends refused to give up, even after two failed tries in a row. They decided to ask their teacher, Ms. Reem, for advice. She told them to think about the kite's shape and the direction of the wind. She said to think about the materials it is made from.

Yousef and Khalid looked at their broken kites closely. They saw that the paper had torn in the strong wind. The sticks had snapped under the pressure.

With this new idea, the boys built a new kite. They used strong plastic, not paper. They used sturdy dowels, not flimsy sticks. They also attached a long tail to help keep the kite steady.

They turned to face the wind, just as Ms. Reem had said. They let the string out slowly. The kite did not break this time, and it did not spin out of control. It rose and flew higher and higher into the sky.

Yousef and Khalid cheered with joy. After trying so many times, their kite could finally fly.

versions.title: The Unbreakable Kite
versions.text:
Have you ever tried something that failed again and again before it finally worked? That is exactly what happened to Yousef and Khalid on Kite Day at their school.

The two friends built their first kite from paper and thin wooden sticks. It was shaped like a simple diamond. Kites can break if their design or materials cannot handle strong wind. That is exactly what happened. The wind gusted hard. The paper tore apart almost instantly. The kite crashed to the ground in pieces.

Determined to succeed, they tried a second kite. It had a slightly different shape. But this one spun wildly instead of climbing steadily. It crashed down just as quickly. Something about their design still was not working.

Rather than give up, Yousef and Khalid asked their science teacher, Ms. Reem, for help. She explained that a good kite needs the right material. It also needs a stable shape, a proper frame, and good balance. She said you also need to launch it facing the correct direction, straight into the wind.

The boys studied their broken kites carefully. They noticed that thin paper tears easily. They saw that thin sticks snap under pressure, especially when a kite is not well balanced.

Using what they learned, they built a brand-new kite. It had a strong plastic cover, a sturdy wooden frame, and a long tail for balance. This time, they faced into the wind. They let the string out slowly, just as their teacher had suggested.

The kite did not tear, and it did not spin out of control. It climbed steadily higher and higher into the sky, flying beautifully above the school field.

Yousef and Khalid cheered with excitement. After two failed attempts, their careful thinking and hard work had finally paid off.

The two friends built their first kite from paper and thin wooden sticks, shaped like a simple diamond. Kites can break if their design or materials cannot handle strong wind, and that is exactly what happened. The wind gusted hard, the paper tore apart almost instantly, and the kite crashed to the ground in pieces.

You also need to launch it facing the correct direction, straight into the wind, so the air can push against it properly.

The boys studied their broken kites and talked about what had gone wrong. They noticed that thin paper tears easily under pressure, and that thin sticks snap when the frame is not strong enough to hold its shape. They also realized that without a tail, a kite has no way to stay balanced once it catches the wind.

Using everything they had learned, the boys built a brand-new kite with a strong plastic cover, a sturdy wooden frame, and a long tail for balance. They faced into the wind and let the string out slowly, exactly as their teacher had suggested.

The kite did not tear, and it did not spin out of control. It climbed steadily higher and higher into the sky, flying beautifully above the entire school field while the other students cheered.

Yousef and Khalid cheered with excitement too. After two failed attempts and plenty of careful thinking, their hard work had finally paid off. They had learned something valuable about how wind, material, and design all work together.

versions.title: The Unbreakable Kite
versions.text:
Have you ever tried something that failed repeatedly before it finally succeeded? That is precisely what happened to Yousef and Khalid on Kite Day at their school, an experience that ultimately taught them a surprising amount about aerodynamics.

The two friends built their first kite from paper and thin wooden sticks, shaped like a simple diamond. Kites can break when their design or materials cannot withstand strong wind, and that is exactly what happened: the wind gusted hard, the paper tore apart almost instantly, and the kite crashed to the ground in pieces.

Determined to succeed, they tried a second kite with a slightly different shape, but this one spun wildly instead of climbing steadily, then crashed down just as quickly. Something about their design was still allowing too much drag and too little lift.

Rather than give up, Yousef and Khalid asked their science teacher, Ms. Reem, for help. She explained that a good kite depends on several things working together: the right material, a stable frame, proper balance, and the correct direction relative to the wind. "The moving air needs to push against the kite's surface," she said, "creating enough lift to carry it upward, while the string provides just enough tension to hold it steady."

The boys studied their broken kites and realized that thin paper tears easily under pressure, and thin sticks snap when a frame cannot hold its shape. They also understood that without a proper tail, a kite has no way to stay balanced once wind resistance begins pulling at it unevenly.

Applying everything they had learned, the boys built a new kite with a strong plastic cover, a sturdy wooden frame, and a carefully measured tail. Facing directly into the wind, they let the string out slowly, feeling the tension increase as the kite caught the air.

The kite did not tear, and it did not spin out of control. Instead, it climbed steadily into the sky, demonstrating exactly the kind of lift Ms. Reem had described, while the other students cheered from below.

Yousef and Khalid's persistence had finally paid off. Two failed attempts had taught them more about wind, material, and design than a single lucky success ever could have.

versions.title: The Unbreakable Kite
versions.text:
Have you ever attempted something that failed repeatedly before it finally succeeded? That is precisely what happened to Yousef and Khalid on Kite Day at their school, an experience that ultimately taught them a surprising amount about aerodynamics, the science of how air moves around objects.

The two friends built their first kite from paper and thin wooden sticks, shaped like a simple diamond. Kites can break when their design or materials cannot withstand strong wind, and that is precisely what happened: the wind gusted hard, the paper tore apart almost instantly, and the kite crashed to the ground in pieces within seconds.

Determined to succeed, they attempted a second kite with a slightly different shape, but this one spun wildly instead of climbing steadily, then crashed down just as quickly. Something about their design was still generating too much drag and far too little lift to keep it airborne.

Rather than give up, Yousef and Khalid asked their science teacher, Ms. Reem, for guidance. She explained that a successful kite depends on several factors working together simultaneously: the right material, a stable frame, proper balance, and the correct direction relative to the prevailing wind. "The moving air needs to push against the kite's surface," she explained, "creating enough lift to carry it upward, while the string provides just enough tension to hold it steady against the pull of the wind."

The boys examined their broken kites and realized that thin paper tears easily under pressure, and thin sticks snap whenever a frame proves unable to maintain its shape. They also understood that without a properly sized tail, a kite has no reliable way to stay balanced once wind resistance begins pulling at it unevenly from different directions.

Applying everything they had learned, the boys constructed an entirely new kite featuring a strong plastic cover, a sturdy wooden frame, and a carefully measured tail nearly a meter long. Facing directly into the wind, they let the string out slowly, feeling the tension steadily increase as the kite caught more and more of the moving air.

This time, the kite did not tear, and it did not spin out of control. Instead, it climbed steadily into the sky, demonstrating precisely the kind of lift that Ms. Reem had described earlier, while the other students cheered enthusiastically from below.

Yousef and Khalid's persistence had finally paid off handsomely. Two failed attempts, rather than discouraging them, had taught them considerably more about wind, material, and design than a single lucky success ever could have.

versions.title: The Unbreakable Kite
versions.text:
Have you ever attempted something that failed repeatedly before it finally succeeded? That is precisely what happened to Yousef and Khalid on Kite Day at their school, an experience that ultimately taught them, through considerable trial and error, a surprising amount about aerodynamics, the science of how moving air interacts with the surfaces of objects passing through it.

The two friends built their first kite from paper and thin wooden sticks, shaped like a simple diamond. Kites can break when their design or materials cannot withstand strong wind, and that is precisely what happened: the wind gusted hard, the paper tore apart almost instantly, and the kite crashed to the ground in pieces within mere seconds.

Determined to succeed nonetheless, they attempted a second kite with a slightly different shape, but this one spun wildly instead of climbing steadily, then crashed down just as quickly as the first. Something about their design was evidently still generating too much drag and far too little lift to keep it reliably airborne.

Rather than abandoning the project, Yousef and Khalid asked their science teacher, Ms. Reem, for guidance. She explained that a successful kite depends on several factors working together simultaneously: the right material, a stable frame, proper balance, and the correct direction relative to the prevailing wind. "The moving air needs to push against the kite's surface," she explained patiently, "creating enough lift to carry it upward, while the string provides just enough tension to hold it steady against the pull of the wind."

The boys examined their two broken kites and realized that thin paper tears easily under pressure, and that thin sticks snap whenever a frame proves unable to maintain its intended shape. They also understood that without a properly sized tail, a kite has no reliable way to stay balanced once wind resistance begins pulling at it unevenly from multiple directions at once.

Applying everything they had learned, the boys constructed an entirely new kite featuring a strong plastic cover, a sturdy wooden frame, and a carefully measured tail nearly a meter long. Facing directly into the wind, they let the string out slowly, feeling the tension steadily increase as the kite caught more and more of the moving air beneath it.

This time, the kite did not tear, and it did not spin out of control. Instead, it climbed steadily into the sky, demonstrating precisely the kind of lift that Ms. Reem had described earlier, while the other students cheered enthusiastically from below, pointing upward in excitement.

Yousef and Khalid's persistence had finally paid off handsomely. Two failed attempts, rather than discouraging them, had taught them considerably more about wind, material, and design than a single lucky success ever could have, and they both agreed that the failures had mattered just as much as the eventual triumph.

versions.title: The Unbreakable Kite
versions.text:
Have you ever attempted something that failed repeatedly before it finally succeeded? That is precisely what happened to Yousef and Khalid on Kite Day at their school, an experience that ultimately taught them, through considerable trial and error, a surprising amount about aerodynamics, the science of how moving air interacts with the surfaces of objects passing through it.

The two friends constructed their first kite from paper and thin wooden sticks, shaped like a simple diamond. Kites can break when their design or materials cannot withstand strong wind, and that is precisely what occurred: the wind gusted hard, the paper tore apart almost instantly, and the kite disintegrated and crashed to the ground in pieces within mere seconds.

Determined to succeed nonetheless, they attempted a second kite with a slightly different shape, but this one spun wildly instead of climbing steadily, then crashed down just as quickly as the first. Something about their underlying design was evidently still generating too much drag and far too little lift to keep it reliably and consistently airborne.

Rather than abandoning the entire project altogether, Yousef and Khalid consulted their science teacher, Ms. Reem, for guidance. She explained that a genuinely successful kite depends on several interdependent factors working together simultaneously: the right material, a stable frame, proper balance, and the correct orientation relative to the prevailing wind conditions. "The moving air needs to push against the kite's surface," she explained patiently, "creating enough lift to carry it upward, while the string provides just enough tension to hold it steady against the pull of the wind."

The boys meticulously examined their two broken kites and realized that thin paper tears easily under pressure, and that thin sticks snap whenever a frame proves structurally unable to maintain its intended shape. They also comprehended that without a properly sized tail, a kite has no reliable way to stay balanced once wind resistance begins pulling at it unevenly from multiple directions at once.

Applying everything they had painstakingly learned, the boys constructed an entirely new kite featuring a durable plastic cover, a sturdy wooden frame, and a carefully measured tail nearly a meter long. Facing directly into the wind, they let the string out slowly, feeling the tension steadily increase as the kite caught more and more of the moving air beneath it.

This time, the kite did not tear, and it did not spin out of control. Instead, it climbed steadily into the sky, demonstrating precisely the kind of aerodynamic lift that Ms. Reem had previously described, while classmates cheered enthusiastically from below, pointing upward with evident excitement.

Yousef and Khalid's persistence had ultimately and handsomely paid off. Two failed attempts, rather than discouraging them, had taught them considerably more about wind, material, and structural design than a single fortunate success ever could have achieved, and they both agreed that the failures had mattered just as much as the eventual triumph. By the end of the day, several other students had asked them for advice, and Yousef and Khalid happily explained what they had discovered about materials, frames, tails, and the invisible forces of lift and drag that shape every successful flight.

Their first kite, built from paper and thin wooden sticks in a simple diamond shape, broke almost immediately: kites can fail when their design or materials cannot withstand strong wind, and the gusting air tore the paper apart within seconds, sending the kite crashing to the ground in pieces. Determined nonetheless, the two friends attempted a second kite with a slightly different shape, but this one spun wildly instead of climbing steadily, then crashed just as quickly, evidently generating too much drag and far too little lift to remain reliably airborne.

Rather than abandoning the project, Yousef and Khalid turned to their science teacher, Ms. Reem, for guidance. She explained that a successful kite depends on several factors working together simultaneously: the right material, a stable frame, proper balance, and the correct direction relative to the prevailing wind. "The moving air needs to push against the kite's surface," she explained, "creating enough lift to carry it upward, while the string provides just enough tension to hold it steady against the pull of the wind." Examining their two broken kites afterward, the boys realized that thin paper tears easily under pressure and thin sticks snap whenever a frame cannot maintain its intended shape, and that without a properly sized tail, a kite has no reliable way to stay balanced once wind resistance begins pulling at it unevenly from multiple directions at once.

Applying everything they had learned, the boys constructed an entirely new kite featuring a strong plastic cover, a sturdy wooden frame, and a carefully measured tail nearly a meter long. Facing directly into the wind, they let the string out slowly, feeling the tension steadily increase as the kite caught more and more of the moving air beneath it. This time, the kite neither tore nor spun out of control; instead, it climbed steadily into the sky, demonstrating precisely the kind of lift that Ms. Reem had described, while the other students cheered enthusiastically from below, pointing upward in excitement.

Yousef and Khalid's persistence had finally paid off handsomely, and both boys agreed that their two failed attempts had taught them considerably more about wind, material, and design than a single lucky success ever could have. By the end of the day, several classmates had approached them for advice, and the two friends happily explained what they had discovered about materials, frames, tails, and the invisible forces of lift and drag that quietly shape every successful flight, whether anyone watching from the ground ever notices them or not.

versions.title: The Unbreakable Kite
versions.text:
Yousef and Khalid discovered a surprising amount about aerodynamics, the branch of science concerned with how moving air interacts with the surfaces of objects passing through it, through an iterative process of repeated failure that eventually produced success on Kite Day. Their first kite, constructed from paper and thin wooden sticks in a simple diamond shape, failed almost immediately: kites can fail structurally when their design or materials cannot withstand strong wind, and the gusting air tore the paper apart within seconds, sending the kite crashing to the ground in pieces. Undeterred, the two friends attempted a second kite with a slightly different shape, but this one spun wildly instead of climbing steadily, then crashed just as quickly, evidently generating excessive drag and insufficient lift to remain reliably airborne.

Rather than abandoning the endeavor altogether, Yousef and Khalid turned to their science teacher, Ms. Reem, for guidance regarding the underlying principles they had clearly misunderstood. She explained that a successful kite depends on several interdependent factors working together simultaneously: appropriate material, a structurally sound frame, proper balance, and the correct orientation relative to the prevailing wind. "The moving air must push against the kite's surface," she explained, "generating sufficient lift to carry it upward, while the string provides just enough tension to hold it steady against the countervailing pull of the wind." Examining their two broken kites afterward, the boys recognized that thin paper tears readily under pressure and thin sticks snap whenever a frame cannot preserve its intended shape, and that without an appropriately sized tail, a kite possesses no reliable mechanism for remaining balanced once wind resistance begins pulling at it unevenly from multiple directions simultaneously.

Applying everything they had learned through this process of trial and error, the boys constructed an entirely new kite featuring a durable plastic covering, a sturdy wooden frame, and a carefully measured tail nearly a meter in length. Facing directly into the wind, they released the string gradually, feeling the tension steadily intensify as the kite captured an increasing volume of moving air beneath its surface. This time, the kite neither tore nor spun uncontrollably; instead, it ascended steadily into the sky, demonstrating precisely the lift that Ms. Reem had described earlier, while classmates cheered enthusiastically from below, pointing upward with evident delight.

Yousef and Khalid's persistence had ultimately paid off considerably, and both boys concluded that their two unsuccessful attempts had taught them far more about wind, material, and structural design than a single fortunate success ever could have achieved. By the conclusion of the day, numerous classmates had approached them seeking advice, and the two friends willingly explained what they had discovered about materials, frames, tails, and the largely invisible forces of lift and drag that quietly govern every successful flight, regardless of whether observers on the ground ever consciously notice them.

keyWords.definition: a light frame covered in paper or cloth that flies in the wind on a string
keyWords.example: We watched a red kite dance high above the beach.
The wind pushed the leaves across the yard.

keyWords.definition: to become damaged or come apart so it stops working
keyWords.example: Be careful, or you might break that glass cup.

keyWords.definition: to put pieces together to make something
keyWords.example: We used blocks to build a tall tower.
Birds fly south when the weather turns cold.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Two friends build many kites until one finally flies well
A class makes a time capsule to open in ten years
A teacher spends the whole story teaching math at school
Two friends spend the whole story building a small robot
questions.why: The story is about Yousef and Khalid building several kites that break or crash until they finally build one that flies.

wrong.B: This describes a different story about a time capsule, not kites.
wrong.C: Ms. Reem teaches science, not math, and the story is not about her lessons in general.
wrong.D: The boys build kites, not a robot.

questions.stem: What happened to the first kite Yousef and Khalid built?
options: It was never fully finished by the boys
It broke because the wind was too strong for the paper
It flew perfectly and smoothly on the very first try
It was much too heavy to lift off the ground
questions.why: In the story, the wind blew hard and the paper kite tore apart.

wrong.A: They did finish building the first kite.
wrong.C: The first kite broke; it did not fly perfectly.
wrong.D: The problem was the wind and materials, not its weight.

questions.stem: What happened to the second kite?
options: It flew higher than any other kite
It got stuck in a tree
It spun around and crashed
It turned into a bird
questions.why: The story says the second kite spun around and fell down fast instead of flying well.

wrong.A: The second kite crashed; it did not fly the highest.
wrong.B: The story does not say it got stuck in a tree.
wrong.D: Kites cannot turn into birds.

questions.stem: Why did their second kite spin and crash?
options: Because there was no wind at all that day
Because Ms. Reem suddenly took the kite away
Because the kite was far too small to see
Because its shape and design still were not right
questions.why: The story explains that something about the kite's shape and design was still not working, which made it spin and crash.

wrong.A: There was wind that day; it was strong enough to tear the first kite.
wrong.B: Ms. Reem helped the boys; she did not take their kite.
wrong.C: Size is not given as the reason for the crash.

questions.stem: In the story, when something breaks, it —
options: gets damaged and stops working properly
grows bigger and stronger than before
becomes much stronger than it was
flies higher into the sky than before
questions.why: In the story, the kites break when the paper tears and the sticks snap, meaning they are damaged and stop working.

wrong.B: Breaking does not make something grow bigger.
wrong.C: Breaking makes something weaker, not stronger.
wrong.D: A broken kite falls; it does not fly higher.

questions.stem: Why do you think Yousef and Khalid asked Ms. Reem for help?
options: Because she owns a small kite shop nearby and sells them new string
Because they could not solve the problem with their kites alone
Because she told them firmly to stop trying and to go home
Because kites of any kind are not allowed at school or in the yard
questions.why: After two kites failed, the boys needed new ideas, so they turned to their teacher for advice.

wrong.A: The story does not say Ms. Reem owns a shop.
wrong.C: Ms. Reem helps them try again; she does not tell them to stop.
wrong.D: The school holds a Kite Day, so kites are clearly allowed.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Yousef and Khalid from the story?
options: They gave up after their first kite broke
They let other students build the kite for them
They kept trying until they solved the problem
They were not interested in kites at all
questions.why: Even after two kites failed, the boys kept trying and eventually built one that flew, showing they did not give up.

wrong.A: They did not give up; they tried a second and third kite.
wrong.B: Yousef and Khalid built the kites themselves.
wrong.D: Their effort shows they cared a great deal about flying a kite.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe both of the kites that broke before showing the kite that worked?
options: To prove that every single kite always breaks eventually
To explain exactly how to fly a real airplane safely
To show that paper kites work better than plastic kites
To show that trying again after failing can lead to success
questions.why: Showing the two failures before the success helps readers see that persistence and learning from mistakes led to the boys' final success.

wrong.A: The final kite does not break, so not all kites break.
wrong.B: The story is about kites, not airplanes.
wrong.C: The final successful kite uses plastic, not paper.

LOW.prompt: Would you want to try building your own kite like Yousef and Khalid? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.

keyWords.definition: the plan or shape of how something is made
keyWords.example: The new car has a sleek, modern design.

keyWords.definition: the substance something is made from
keyWords.example: Cotton is a soft material used for making shirts.

keyWords.definition: the way something is pointing or moving toward
keyWords.example: The hikers checked a map to find the right direction.

keyWords.definition: the structure that holds something together and gives it shape
keyWords.example: The picture hung inside a wooden frame.

keyWords.definition: a steady state where something does not tip over to one side
keyWords.example: The gymnast kept her balance while walking on the beam.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Yousef and Khalid learn what makes a kite fly well.
Yousef and Khalid learn how to swim at the pool.
Yousef and Khalid build a small treehouse together.
Yousef and Khalid compete in a long running race.
questions.why: The article follows Yousef and Khalid as their early kites fail, until they learn what a kite needs to fly successfully.

wrong.B: The article never mentions swimming.
wrong.C: The article is about kites, not a treehouse.
wrong.D: The article does not describe a race.

questions.stem: According to Ms. Reem, what four things does a good kite need?
options: speed, color, size, and the total weight of the whole kite
the right material, a stable frame, good balance, and wind direction
a small motor, wheels, lights, and a remote control for the kite
glue, paint, extra string, and a name tag for the owner
questions.why: Ms. Reem explains that a good kite needs the right material, a stable frame, good balance, and the correct wind direction.

wrong.A: The article does not list these as requirements.
wrong.C: Kites in the article do not have motors or remote controls.
wrong.D: These items are not mentioned as requirements for the kite.

questions.stem: What material did the boys use for their final, successful kite's cover?
options: cloth
cardboard
plastic
metal
questions.why: In the article, the boys built their final kite with a strong plastic cover.

wrong.A: The article does not mention cloth.
wrong.B: The article does not mention cardboard.
wrong.D: The article does not mention metal for the cover.

questions.stem: Put the events of the story in the correct order.
options: The kite flies; the first kite breaks; the second kite spins
The second kite spins; the kite flies; the first kite breaks
The first kite breaks; the kite flies; the second kite spins
The first kite breaks; the second kite spins; the kite flies
questions.why: The first kite breaks, then the second kite spins and crashes, and only afterward does the final kite fly successfully.

wrong.A: The kite cannot fly before the first kite even breaks.
wrong.B: The first kite must break before the second kite is even built.
wrong.C: The second kite spins before the final kite flies, not after.

questions.stem: In the story, the word balance means —
options: staying steady and not tipping to one side
moving very fast and wildly through the air
a rare type of wind that blows sideways
the total price of building a brand new kite
questions.why: The article uses balance to describe staying steady, which the tail helps the kite do once it catches the wind.

wrong.B: Balance is not about speed.
wrong.C: Balance is not a type of wind.
wrong.D: Balance has nothing to do with price.

questions.stem: Why did the boys add a long tail to their new kite?
options: To make the kite much heavier overall
To help the kite stay balanced in the wind
To make the kite look prettier for the day
To slow the kite down completely in flight
questions.why: In the story, the long tail helps the kite stay balanced in the wind.

wrong.A: The tail's purpose in the article is balance, not extra weight.
wrong.C: The article gives a functional reason, not just appearance.
wrong.D: The tail helps it fly steadily, not stop it from flying.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why the boys tested the kite's materials and frame before flying it again?
options: They wanted to waste a whole afternoon because they had nothing else to do
They did not trust Ms. Reem's careful advice about the wind and string
They wanted to understand their mistakes so the next kite would not fail
They were simply told to do so by classmates who watched them fail
questions.why: By studying what went wrong with the broken kites, the boys could avoid repeating the same mistakes in their next attempt.

wrong.A: Their careful study helped them succeed; it was not wasted time.
wrong.B: They followed Ms. Reem's advice closely in building the new kite.
wrong.D: The article does not mention classmates giving them instructions.

questions.stem: How is the boys' first kite different from their final kite?
options: The first kite was much bigger and heavier than the final one, and had a longer string
The first kite flew much higher than the final kite did on both of the days
The first kite had a tail, but the final kite did not have one at all
The first kite used weak paper, while the final kite used strong plastic
questions.why: The first kite was made of paper and thin sticks that failed, while the final kite used strong plastic and a sturdy wooden frame.

wrong.A: The article does not compare the size or weight of the two kites.
wrong.B: The first kite crashed; it did not fly higher than the final one.
wrong.C: The final kite has the tail; the first kite did not.

MID.prompt: Explain how Yousef and Khalid solved the problem with their kite. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained how the boys solved their problem.
I used at least two details from the article.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.

keyWords.definition: the science of how air moves around and interacts with objects
keyWords.example: Engineers study aerodynamics to design faster cars.

keyWords.definition: the upward force created when moving air pushes against a surface
keyWords.example: An airplane's wings are shaped to create enough lift to rise into the sky.

keyWords.definition: the force created when something is pulled or stretched tight
keyWords.example: The tightrope walker depended on the tension in the wire.

keyWords.definition: the force of air resistance that slows a moving object down
keyWords.example: Streamlined cars are designed to reduce drag as they drive fast.

keyWords.definition: the quality of continuing to try, even after failing
keyWords.example: Her persistence paid off when she finally learned to ride a bicycle.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the article?
options: Through failure and problem-solving, the boys come to understand aerodynamics.
Kites are far too dangerous and should never be flown at school, even on calm days.
Only very expensive kites made of solid metal can ever fly in the open air.
Ms. Reem secretly built the winning kite for the two boys the night before.
questions.why: The article traces how the boys' repeated failures and careful thinking lead them to understand what makes a kite fly.

wrong.B: The article presents kite-flying as a fun school activity, not a danger.
wrong.C: The successful kite uses plastic and wood, not metal.
wrong.D: Ms. Reem gives advice, but the boys build the kite themselves.

questions.stem: Why did the boys' second kite generate too much drag and too little lift?
options: Because it was painted an unusual bright color by the boys at home
Because something about its shape and design was still not right
Because there was no wind at all on Kite Day at the park
Because it was flown indoors inside the gym of the school
questions.why: The article explains that something about the second kite's shape and design was still not working properly, causing too much drag and too little lift.

wrong.A: Color is never mentioned as a factor.
wrong.C: There was plenty of wind, which is partly why the kites failed.
wrong.D: Kite Day takes place outdoors on the school field.

questions.stem: According to Ms. Reem, what does the string provide to keep the kite steady?
options: extra weight for the frame of the kite
a bright color so the string can be seen
tension against the pull of the wind
a small source of light for the night
questions.why: Ms. Reem explains that the string provides just enough tension to hold the kite steady against the pull of the wind.

wrong.A: The string is not described as providing weight.
wrong.B: The string's color is not discussed.
wrong.D: The string does not provide light.

questions.stem: In the article, the word persistence means —
options: giving up quickly after one failure at a task
the shape of a kite's frame and its tail
a strong gust of wind that lifts a kite
continuing to try despite repeated failure
questions.why: The article uses persistence to describe how the boys kept trying even after two kites failed, which finally paid off.

wrong.A: Persistence is the opposite of giving up.
wrong.B: Persistence describes an attitude, not a shape.
wrong.C: Persistence is not a type of wind.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why Ms. Reem explained the science behind kites rather than simply building one for the boys?
options: She wanted them to understand their failures and solve it themselves
She did not know how to build a kite herself at all, so she gave a lecture
She secretly wanted the boys to fail a third time so they would give up
She firmly believed that only adults should ever fly kites in the open fields
questions.why: By explaining the science rather than building the kite herself, Ms. Reem helped the boys learn to solve the problem on their own.

wrong.B: The article does not suggest she lacks this knowledge.
wrong.C: She helps them succeed, not fail again.
wrong.D: The article never claims only adults should fly kites.

questions.stem: Which best describes the order of events in the article?
options: The final kite flies; the first kite breaks; Ms. Reem gives advice; the second kite crashes
The first kite breaks; the second kite crashes; Ms. Reem gives advice; the final kite flies
Ms. Reem gives advice; the final kite flies; the first kite breaks; the second kite crashes
The second kite crashes; the final kite flies; the first kite breaks; Ms. Reem gives advice
questions.why: The first kite breaks, the second kite crashes, Ms. Reem then gives advice, and only after that does the final kite fly successfully.

wrong.A: The final kite cannot fly before the first kite even breaks.
wrong.C: The first kite must break before Ms. Reem is even asked for advice.
wrong.D: The second kite crashes before the final kite flies, not after.

questions.stem: How does the article compare lift and drag in a kite's flight?
options: It claims that drag is always more useful than lift
It claims that lift and drag are exactly the same force
It shows that lift must rise while too much drag stops good flight
It claims that only adult kites ever experience lift and drag
questions.why: The article shows that the final kite succeeds because it generates enough lift, while the earlier kites failed partly because of too much drag.

wrong.A: The article never claims drag is more useful than lift.
wrong.B: Lift and drag are described as different forces with different effects.
wrong.D: Lift and drag apply to any kite, not only adult kites.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article by describing Yousef and Khalid explaining their discovery to classmates?
options: To suggest that only teachers should ever explain science
To argue that all kite-flying should be banned at school
To show that their classmates were uninterested in kites
To emphasize that what they learned was valuable enough to share
questions.why: Ending with the boys sharing their discovery shows that their hard-won knowledge about kites was valuable enough to pass on to others.

wrong.A: The boys themselves explain the science, not only teachers.
wrong.B: The article celebrates kite-flying rather than arguing against it.
wrong.C: Classmates approach them for advice, showing clear interest.

HIGH.prompt: Do you think persistence was more important than scientific knowledge in helping Yousef and Khalid succeed, or were both equally important? Support your argument with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported my position with specific evidence from the article.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.

LOW.stem: What did Ms. Reem tell the boys to think about?
options: How much the kite costs at a big store
How many of their friends could fly it
What color the long kite string should be
The shape of the kite and what it is made of
LOW.why: In the story, Ms. Reem told the boys to think about the kite's shape and what it is made of.

wrong.A: She did not talk about the cost of a kite.
wrong.B: She did not talk about how many friends could fly it.
wrong.C: She did not talk about the string color.

LOW.stem: In the story, what does "give up" mean?
options: Give a nice gift to a friend
Stop trying to do something
Start a brand new school day
Fly a kite up very high today
LOW.why: The boys did not give up, and they kept trying until their kite flew.

wrong.A: The story is not about giving gifts.
wrong.C: It has nothing to do with starting a school day.
wrong.D: The boys fly the kite at the end, but that is not what the words mean.

LOW.stem: What helped the boys most to make a kite that flew?
options: They learned from their old kites
They waited for a day with no wind
They asked a friend to fly it
They painted the kite a bright color
LOW.why: The boys looked at their old kites, saw why they broke, and then built a stronger one.

wrong.B: The kite flew in the wind, so they did not wait for no wind.
wrong.C: No friend flies the kite for them in the story.
wrong.D: The story does not say anything about paint.

LOW.stem: How did the boys let out the string?
options: Very fast and hard
In the middle of the night
Slowly
With a big tail
LOW.why: The text says, "They let the string out slowly."

wrong.A: They did not pull the string fast.
wrong.B: The story is set on Kite Day at school, not at night.
wrong.D: The tail is on the kite, not a way of letting out the string.

MID.stem: According to Ms. Reem, which way should you face when you launch a kite?
options: Away from the wind
Straight into the wind
Toward the school field
Up at the sun
MID.why: She said you need to launch it facing straight into the wind.

wrong.A: She said to face into the wind, not away from it.
wrong.C: The field is where the kite flies, not the direction she gave.
wrong.D: She never mentions the sun.

MID.stem: In the article, what does the word "determined" mean?
options: Scared of the strong wind outside
Bored with the whole kite game
Firmly decided to keep trying
Surprised by a very new idea
MID.why: After the first kite crashed, the boys were determined to succeed, so they built a second one.

wrong.A: The boys keep building, so they are not scared.
wrong.B: They were working hard, not bored.
wrong.D: They were not surprised; they wanted to succeed.

MID.stem: Why does the author start the article with a question?
options: To test whether readers already know how to build kites
To tell readers all the rules for Kite Day at school
To list all the parts that make up a good kite
To make readers think about their own failures and success
MID.why: The question asks if you ever failed before you finally succeeded, which connects the reader to the boys' story.

wrong.A: The question is not a test of kite skills.
wrong.B: The rules of Kite Day are never listed.
wrong.C: The parts of a kite are explained later by Ms. Reem.

MID.stem: What does the last paragraph suggest about failing at first?
options: It can lead to success when you keep learning
It means you should choose a new game
It happens only to people who do not try
It is the fault of the wind
MID.why: The boys failed twice, and their careful thinking and hard work finally paid off.

wrong.B: The boys did not change games; they kept trying.
wrong.C: The boys tried hard and still failed at first.
wrong.D: The article says the design and materials were the problem.

HIGH.stem: What did the boys realize about the thin sticks in their broken kites?
options: They were far too heavy for the thin paper cover
They were painted the wrong color
They snapped when the frame could not hold its shape
They were too long for the string
HIGH.why: In the text, thin sticks snap when a frame cannot hold its shape.

wrong.A: The sticks were thin, not heavy.
wrong.B: Color is never mentioned.
wrong.D: Length is never mentioned as a problem.

HIGH.stem: According to the article, why does a kite without a proper tail have trouble?
options: It cannot stay balanced when the wind pulls on it unevenly
It becomes too heavy to climb into the sky above the field
It makes the string tangle on the ground
It tears the paper at the center
HIGH.why: The boys understood that without a tail, a kite cannot stay balanced when wind resistance pulls unevenly.

wrong.B: The article does not say a tail adds too much weight.
wrong.C: String tangles are not mentioned.
wrong.D: The tail is linked to balance, not to tearing paper.

HIGH.stem: In the article, the word "withstand" most nearly means —
options: to copy another kite exactly
to hide
to repair
to handle without breaking
HIGH.why: Kites break when their design or materials cannot withstand strong wind, so the word means to handle the wind without breaking.

wrong.A: Copying a kite is not what the sentence is about.
wrong.B: Hiding does not fit with strong wind.
wrong.C: Repairing happens after a kite breaks, not before.

HIGH.stem: What does the last sentence suggest about learning from mistakes?
options: Luck is the best way to learn anything new
Failed attempts can teach more than one lucky success
Two tries are always enough to make anything work
It is best to avoid trying new designs
HIGH.why: The author says two failed attempts taught the boys more than a single lucky success could have.

wrong.A: The author says a lucky success teaches less.
wrong.C: The boys needed three tries, not two.
wrong.D: The boys learned by trying new designs.
